titolo: The 72-hour myth: does pizza digestibility really depend on fermentation?
sintesi: Pizza digestibility is often attributed to endless maturation times that would 'predigest' gluten. Gastric physiology and food biochemistry, however, demonstrate a very different reality: starch digestion depends on proper baking, while gluten is broken down by gastric pepsin, not by the enzymes in the flour at low temperatures.
corpo: In the pizza world, there is a widespread belief that dough matured for 48 or 72 hours in the refrigerator is intrinsically more digestible because the enzymes in the flour would have 'broken down the gluten' in place of our stomach. From a scientific standpoint, this is a myth: the plant proteases in flour at 4°C hydrolyze only 1-2% of gluten's peptide bonds, just enough to relax the mesh and facilitate stretching by the pizzaiolo. The human digestive system, thanks to hydrochloric acid and pepsin in the stomach (and subsequently pancreatic trypsin), breaks down proteins with incomparably higher efficiency, making the alleged 'cold predigestion' physiologically irrelevant. At the same time, the digestibility of starches — which make up over 70% of the flour — does not depend on hours of fermentation, but on their complete thermal gelatinization during baking: a pizza that is poorly baked or moist in the center will be indigestible regardless of maturation days. Finally, the typical heaviness or nighttime thirst does not stem from still-living yeast (which die instantly above 55-60°C in the oven), but from the high salt concentration in the dough and toppings and from the cooked fats in dairy products that slow gastric emptying.
